AEROSPACE, SECURITY AND DEFENCE INDUSTRIES ASSOCIATION OF EUROPE AEROSPACE, SECURITY AND DEFENCE INDUSTRIES ASSOCIATION OF EUROPE 20010131 Bike book BY13 S1000D upissued CPF_2020-040EPWG Bike Enhancement with elements and attributes missing in the samples Brake system The most important part of the bicycle is the brake system. Only a minimum maintenance of the brake system is necessary. But, when a problem does occur, make sure you to do the necessary maintenance as quickly as possible. If you do not do this the bicycle will be dangerous to use. There are nine different types of brake systems. The one found on most bicycles is the cantileverbrake (refer to ). Cantilever brake The brake system (refer to ) has these primary components: the brake lever (refer to ) the brake cable the brake arm the brake clamp (also known as callipers) the brake pads (refer to ) A cable that goes from the brake levers on the handlebars pulls the two levers on the brakes together. This presses the brake pads against the outer rim of the wheel, which decreases the speed of the bicycle. Brake pads There are four brake pads (refer to ) on the bicycle. Two are found on the front wheel and two on the rear wheel. The brake pads are made out of hard wearing rubber. The pads press against the rim of the wheel to cause friction when the you operate the brake levers. Brake lever The brake levers (refer to ) are easily damaged. The lever is installed in the mount. A clamp bolt holds the mount. This bolt is not visible because it is found in the mount. The lever turns on a lever pivot bolt. The adjuster lock nut holds the brake cable. This lock nut adjusts the tension of the cable. The left brake lever holds the brake pads on the front wheel and the right brake pads hold the brakes on the rear wheel.

                     <brCategoryGroup>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat010">
                           <title>Data output business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Data output business rules specify the output formats for S1000D data. These formats can include page-oriented (eg, paper, pdf) formats, IETP formats, multimedia formats and SCORM formats. The decision regarding which portion of the data will be published in what formats must be agreed and written within these business rules.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat004">
                           <title>Security business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Security business rules cover all security issues and intellectual property rights. They include security classifications, copyright markings, use or disclosure restrictions, destruction instructions and any other data restrictions.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat007">
                           <title>Data exchange business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>The rules for how data must be exchanged between partners and customers are covered in business rule category 7. This includes for example the use of data dispatch notes and how data management requirement lists as well as CSDB status lists are used. The rules in this category include how the S1000D file based transfer protocol is used, the frequency of data exchanges, if unverified data are exchanged, the rules for data module and graphic issue numbers, and the acceptance and rejection criteria.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="BRDPgroup01">
                           <title>BRDP group 1: General managerial decisions</title>
                        </brCategory>

                     <brDecisionPointText>
                        <para>Decide on the strategy for legends. Legends can appear as part of the illustration or as text using the element <legend>.                            <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Text creation business rules consist of rules and guidelines (including terminology rules such as language and dictionaries, and the order of preference) for maximizing the amount of reuse that can be achieved within technical publications, and between technical publications and supporting training content.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat010">
                           <title>Data output business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Data output business rules specify the output formats for S1000D data. These formats can include page-oriented (eg, paper, pdf) formats, IETP formats, multimedia formats and SCORM formats. The decision regarding which portion of the data will be published in what formats must be agreed and written within these business rules.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat005">
                           <title>Business process business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Business process business rules cover how technical publications development is coordinated with other disciplines within an organization or within the project level at that organization or the project as a whole. For example, they describe the rules and relationships with LSA, S2000M compliant initial provisioning, engineering/design and training (eg, SCORM conformance).</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat007">
                           <title>Data exchange business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>The rules for how data must be exchanged between partners and customers are covered in business rule category 7. This includes for example the use of data dispatch notes and how data management requirement lists as well as CSDB status lists are used. The rules in this category include how the S1000D file based transfer protocol is used, the frequency of data exchanges, if unverified data are exchanged, the rules for data module and graphic issue numbers, and the acceptance and rejection criteria.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat008">
                           <title>Data integrity and management business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Data integrity and management business rules enforce the referential integrity within the CSDB. Closely coupled with the data exchange business rules they cover how data is managed by both the creator and the customer.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat009">
                           <title>Legacy data conversion, management and handling business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Legacy data conversion, management and handling business rules are quite separate from the other categories outlined above and can be considered (to some extent) as being outside of the scope of S1000D. They cover rules for converting data from say, an ATA iSpec 2200 project, to data modules and will vary from project to project depending on the format of the source data (word processor, paper, Standard Generalized Markup Language (SGML)), and how the target data modules must be treated.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="BRDPgroup14">
                           <title>BRDP group 14: Referencing</title>
                        </brCategory>
                     </brCategoryGroup>
                  </brRelatedTo>

                     <brCategoryGroup>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat006a">
                           <title>Data creation business rules - Text</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Text creation business rules consist of rules and guidelines (including terminology rules such as language and dictionaries, and the order of preference) for maximizing the amount of reuse that can be achieved within technical publications, and between technical publications and supporting training content.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat010">
                           <title>Data output business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Data output business rules specify the output formats for S1000D data. These formats can include page-oriented (eg, paper, pdf) formats, IETP formats, multimedia formats and SCORM formats. The decision regarding which portion of the data will be published in what formats must be agreed and written within these business rules.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat005">
                           <title>Business process business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Business process business rules cover how technical publications development is coordinated with other disciplines within an organization or within the project level at that organization or the project as a whole. For example, they describe the rules and relationships with LSA, S2000M compliant initial provisioning, engineering/design and training (eg, SCORM conformance).</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat007">
                           <title>Data exchange business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>The rules for how data must be exchanged between partners and customers are covered in business rule category 7. This includes for example the use of data dispatch notes and how data management requirement lists as well as CSDB status lists are used. The rules in this category include how the S1000D file based transfer protocol is used, the frequency of data exchanges, if unverified data are exchanged, the rules for data module and graphic issue numbers, and the acceptance and rejection criteria.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat008">
                           <title>Data integrity and management business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Data integrity and management business rules enforce the referential integrity within the CSDB. Closely coupled with the data exchange business rules they cover how data is managed by both the creator and the customer.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat009">
                           <title>Legacy data conversion, management and handling business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Legacy data conversion, management and handling business rules are quite separate from the other categories outlined above and can be considered (to some extent) as being outside of the scope of S1000D. They cover rules for converting data from say, an ATA iSpec 2200 project, to data modules and will vary from project to project depending on the format of the source data (word processor, paper, Standard Generalized Markup Language (SGML)), and how the target data modules must be treated.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="BRDPgroup14">
                           <title>BRDP group 14: Referencing</title>
                        </brCategory>
                     </brCategoryGroup>

                     <brCategoryGroup>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat006a">
                           <title>Data creation business rules - Text</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Text creation business rules consist of rules and guidelines (including terminology rules such as language and dictionaries, and the order of preference) for maximizing the amount of reuse that can be achieved within technical publications, and between technical publications and supporting training content.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat002">
                           <title>Product definition business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Product definition business rules cover the data module coding strategy related to how the Product is broken down (eg, physical or functional). Included is the definition of the model identification codes to be used in the Product and its subsystems. Supplier subsystems and identifications also need to be considered.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat003">
                           <title>Maintenance philosophy and concepts of operation business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Maintenance philosophy and concepts of operation business rules cover the types of information that a project or an organization requires. They include for example a list or detailed specification of chosen information sets, an information codes specification which details the information codes, and information names that describe the data module content.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat004">
                           <title>Security business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Security business rules cover all security issues and intellectual property rights. They include security classifications, copyright markings, use or disclosure restrictions, destruction instructions and any other data restrictions.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat005">
                           <title>Business process business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Business process business rules cover how technical publications development is coordinated with other disciplines within an organization or within the project level at that organization or the project as a whole. For example, they describe the rules and relationships with LSA, S2000M compliant initial provisioning, engineering/design and training (eg, SCORM conformance).</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat009">
                           <title>Legacy data conversion, management and handling business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Legacy data conversion, management and handling business rules are quite separate from the other categories outlined above and can be considered (to some extent) as being outside of the scope of S1000D. They cover rules for converting data from say, an ATA iSpec 2200 project, to data modules and will vary from project to project depending on the format of the source data (word processor, paper, Standard Generalized Markup Language (SGML)), and how the target data modules must be treated.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="BRDPgroup31">
                           <title>BRDP group 31: Illustrated parts data (Information set, publications, Schema details, data module type)</title>

                           <brCategoryDescription>

                     <brDecisionPointText>
                        <para>Decide on the strategy for legends. Legends can appear as part of the illustration or as text using the element <legend>.                         <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat010">
                           <title>Data output business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Data output business rules specify the output formats for S1000D data. These formats can include page-oriented (eg, paper, pdf) formats, IETP formats, multimedia formats and SCORM formats. The decision regarding which portion of the data will be published in what formats must be agreed and written within these business rules.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat005">
                           <title>Business process business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Business process business rules cover how technical publications development is coordinated with other disciplines within an organization or within the project level at that organization or the project as a whole. For example, they describe the rules and relationships with LSA, S2000M compliant initial provisioning, engineering/design and training (eg, SCORM conformance).</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat007">
                           <title>Data exchange business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>The rules for how data must be exchanged between partners and customers are covered in business rule category 7. This includes for example the use of data dispatch notes and how data management requirement lists as well as CSDB status lists are used. The rules in this category include how the S1000D file based transfer protocol is used, the frequency of data exchanges, if unverified data are exchanged, the rules for data module and graphic issue numbers, and the acceptance and rejection criteria.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat008">
                           <title>Data integrity and management business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Data integrity and management business rules enforce the referential integrity within the CSDB. Closely coupled with the data exchange business rules they cover how data is managed by both the creator and the customer.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat009">
                           <title>Legacy data conversion, management and handling business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Legacy data conversion, management and handling business rules are quite separate from the other categories outlined above and can be considered (to some extent) as being outside of the scope of S1000D. They cover rules for converting data from say, an ATA iSpec 2200 project, to data modules and will vary from project to project depending on the format of the source data (word processor, paper, Standard Generalized Markup Language (SGML)), and how the target data modules must be treated.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="BRDPgroup14">
                           <title>BRDP group 14: Referencing</title>
                        </brCategory>
                     </brCategoryGroup>
                  </brRelatedTo>
                  <brDecisionPointContent>

                     <brDecisionPointText>

                     </brDecisionPointText>

                     <brCategoryGroup>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat006a">
                           <title>Data creation business rules - Text</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Text creation business rules consist of rules and guidelines (including terminology rules such as language and dictionaries, and the order of preference) for maximizing the amount of reuse that can be achieved within technical publications, and between technical publications and supporting training content.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat010">
                           <title>Data output business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Data output business rules specify the output formats for S1000D data. These formats can include page-oriented (eg, paper, pdf) formats, IETP formats, multimedia formats and SCORM formats. The decision regarding which portion of the data will be published in what formats must be agreed and written within these business rules.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat005">
                           <title>Business process business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Business process business rules cover how technical publications development is coordinated with other disciplines within an organization or within the project level at that organization or the project as a whole. For example, they describe the rules and relationships with LSA, S2000M compliant initial provisioning, engineering/design and training (eg, SCORM conformance).</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat007">
                           <title>Data exchange business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>The rules for how data must be exchanged between partners and customers are covered in business rule category 7. This includes for example the use of data dispatch notes and how data management requirement lists as well as CSDB status lists are used. The rules in this category include how the S1000D file based transfer protocol is used, the frequency of data exchanges, if unverified data are exchanged, the rules for data module and graphic issue numbers, and the acceptance and rejection criteria.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat008">
                           <title>Data integrity and management business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Data integrity and management business rules enforce the referential integrity within the CSDB. Closely coupled with the data exchange business rules they cover how data is managed by both the creator and the customer.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat009">
                           <title>Legacy data conversion, management and handling business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Legacy data conversion, management and handling business rules are quite separate from the other categories outlined above and can be considered (to some extent) as being outside of the scope of S1000D. They cover rules for converting data from say, an ATA iSpec 2200 project, to data modules and will vary from project to project depending on the format of the source data (word processor, paper, Standard Generalized Markup Language (SGML)), and how the target data modules must be treated.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="BRDPgroup14">
                           <title>BRDP group 14: Referencing</title>
                        </brCategory>
                     </brCategoryGroup>
                  </brRelatedTo>

                     <brDecisionPointText>
                        <para>Decide whether to use the attribute pubCodingScheme. If used, decide on the set of allowed coding schemes and the syntax of those schemes.</para>

                     <sourceDocRef>

                              </dmTitle>
                           </dmRefAddressItems>
                        </dmRef>
                     </sourceDocRef>
                     <brCategoryGroup>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat006a">
                           <title>Data creation business rules - Text</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Text creation business rules consist of rules and guidelines (including terminology rules such as language and dictionaries, and the order of preference) for maximizing the amount of reuse that can be achieved within technical publications, and between technical publications and supporting training content.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat002">
                           <title>Product definition business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Product definition business rules cover the data module coding strategy related to how the Product is broken down (eg, physical or functional). Included is the definition of the model identification codes to be used in the Product and its subsystems. Supplier subsystems and identifications also need to be considered.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat003">
                           <title>Maintenance philosophy and concepts of operation business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Maintenance philosophy and concepts of operation business rules cover the types of information that a project or an organization requires. They include for example a list or detailed specification of chosen information sets, an information codes specification which details the information codes, and information names that describe the data module content.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat004">
                           <title>Security business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Security business rules cover all security issues and intellectual property rights. They include security classifications, copyright markings, use or disclosure restrictions, destruction instructions and any other data restrictions.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat005">
                           <title>Business process business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Business process business rules cover how technical publications development is coordinated with other disciplines within an organization or within the project level at that organization or the project as a whole. For example, they describe the rules and relationships with LSA, S2000M compliant initial provisioning, engineering/design and training (eg, SCORM conformance).</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="Cat009">
                           <title>Legacy data conversion, management and handling business rules</title>
                           <brCategoryDescription>
                              <para>Legacy data conversion, management and handling business rules are quite separate from the other categories outlined above and can be considered (to some extent) as being outside of the scope of S1000D. They cover rules for converting data from say, an ATA iSpec 2200 project, to data modules and will vary from project to project depending on the format of the source data (word processor, paper, Standard Generalized Markup Language (SGML)), and how the target data modules must be treated.</para>
                           </brCategoryDescription>
                        </brCategory>
                        <brCategory brCategoryNumber="BRDPgroup31">
                           <title>BRDP group 31: Illustrated parts data (Information set, publications, Schema details, data module type)</title>
                        </brCategory>
                     </brCategoryGroup>
                  </brRelatedTo>

AEROSPACE, SECURITY AND DEFENCE INDUSTRIES ASSOCIATION OF EUROPE AEROSPACE, SECURITY AND DEFENCE INDUSTRIES ASSOCIATION OF EUROPE Mountain bicycle and (Mountain storm Mk1 or Brook trekker Mk9) 20010131 Bike book BY S1000D upissued CPF_2016-016NL S1000D DIG SVG Profile Recommendation CGM replaced by SVG CPF_2020-040EPWG Bike Enhancement with elements and attributes missing in the samples foldout Physical description of a bicycle A bicycle (refer to ) is a frame and a number of movable components with mechanical parts that are completely open. There are no covers or sheet metal panels that prevent access to the mechanical parts. Thus, you can disassemble the different components of a bicycle (refer to ) to do: an inspection a maintenance task a repair task The parts that you can immediately identify on a bicycle are given in . Bicycle parts Item Refer to Definition All parts can be procured from any certified part distributor Frame A bicycle frame is made of metal tubes that are welded together. Wheels The wheels include these parts: Hub Spokes Metal rim Rubber tire Rear wheel Front wheel Seat and seat post These install into the seat tube with a mechanism you can use to change the height. Handle bars A horizontal bar that attaches to the stem with grips at the ends that attach to the brake levers and the shifters. Handle bar stem This attaches the handle bar to the steering tube (head set). Cranks A lever that extends from the bottom of the bracket to the pedal. Pedals The two platforms for the feet that attach to the crank. Chain A circular set of links that connect the chain ring to the cogs on the freewheel. Gears The gears include: Front chain ring Rear freewheel Front and the rear derailleur Shift lever on the handle bars Cables Brakes The brakes include: Actuators on the handlebars Brake cable Brake callipers Brake pads

      <description>
         <levelledPara>
            <title>Quick history of the bicycle</title>
            
            <para>Here are the most important steps in the invention of the bicycle:<sequentialList id="SPEC-0008">
                  <listItem>
                     <para>In 1817 a German professor, baron Karl von Drais, created the first two-wheeled bicycle. It had a handlebar, and looked like a bicycle of today, but it didn't have pedals, and it had a wooden body.</para>
                  </listItem>
                  <listItem>
                     <para>In the 1860s, French inventors added pedals to the front wheel. However, it took a lot of effort to turn the pedals. Later inventors made bikes out of metal only, and made the front wheel very big, giving higher speed. This design was called the penny-farthing bicycle. However, it was difficult to ride, since it could fall easily.</para>
                  </listItem>
                  <listItem>
                     <para>Several improvements were made in the 1880s and '90s. In 1885, the safety bicycle was invented. This had two wheels the same size so that the rider could sit at a lower height. It was called the safety bicycle because it was much easier to ride than the penny-farthing. Instead of pedaling and steering with the front wheel, the safety bicycle used steering with the front wheel while the pedals turned the back wheel using a chain. Brakes operated by hand levers on some bikes also increased safety.</para>
                  </listItem>
                  <listItem>
                     <para>In 1888, Scottish inventor John Boyd Dunlop re-invented a type of tire which was filled with air, and this made cycling far more comfortable.</para>
                  </listItem>
                  <listItem>
                     <para>Soon, the freewheel was invented. This was a device inside the hub of the back wheel that allowed the wheel to spin even if the rider wasn't pedalling. However, this meant the rider could no longer stop the bike by backpedalling. As a result, a different type of brake was invented which could stop the bike if the pedals were turned backwards. Later inventions included better brakes, and gears, which made cycling over hills much easier.</para>
                  </listItem>
                  <listItem>
                     <note>
                        <notePara>During this time the bicycle became very popular. Long-distance racing are quickly developing:<attentionSequentialList id="SPEC-0004">
                              <attentionSequentialListItem id="SPEC-0005">
                                 <attentionListItemPara id="SPEC-0001">Paris-Rouen, as soon as 1869</attentionListItemPara>
                              </attentionSequentialListItem>
                              <attentionSequentialListItem>
                                 <attentionListItemPara>Bordeaux-Paris, in May 1891</attentionListItemPara>
                              </attentionSequentialListItem>
                              <attentionSequentialListItem>
                                 <attentionListItemPara>Paris-Brest-Paris, in September 1891</attentionListItemPara>
                              </attentionSequentialListItem>
                              <attentionSequentialListItem>
                                 <attentionListItemPara>Liège-Bastogne-Liège, in 1892</attentionListItemPara>
                              </attentionSequentialListItem>
                              <attentionSequentialListItem>
                                 <attentionListItemPara>Paris-Roubaix, in 1896</attentionListItemPara>
                              </attentionSequentialListItem>
                              <attentionSequentialListItem>
                                 <attentionListItemPara>Tour de France, in 1903</attentionListItemPara>
                              </attentionSequentialListItem>
                           </attentionSequentialList>
                        </notePara>
                        
                     </note>
                  </listItem>
               </sequentialList>
               <verbatimText id="SPEC-0009">Source: https://en.vikidia.org/w/index.php?title=Bicycle&oldid=97889</verbatimText>
            </para>
            
            <note>
               <notePara>Bicycles are nowadays one of the main means of transportation in many parts of the world. Its energy efficiency is particularly high. Its practice, cycling, is both<attentionRandomList>
                     <attentionRandomListItem id="SPEC-0003">
                        <attentionListItemPara id="SPEC-0002">a daily use of transport,</attentionListItemPara>
                     </attentionRandomListItem>
                     <attentionRandomListItem>
                        <attentionListItemPara>a popular hobby,</attentionListItemPara>
                     </attentionRandomListItem>
                     <attentionRandomListItem>
                        <attentionListItemPara>and a sport.</attentionListItemPara>
                     </attentionRandomListItem>
                  </attentionRandomList>
                  <verbatimText id="SPEC-0010">Source: https://fr.vikidia.org/w/index.php?title=V%C3%A9lo&oldid=1427276</verbatimText>
               </notePara>
               
            </note>
         </levelledPara>
         <levelledPara>
            <title>Functional description of a bicycle</title>
            <para>Below is a list of the different bicycle components and a functional description of them. <definitionList>
                  <definitionListHeader>
                     <termTitle>Component</termTitle>
                     <definitionTitle>Functional description</definitionTitle>
                  </definitionListHeader>
                  
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Frame</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The frame is the skeleton of the bicycle. Refer to <dmRef>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA3" subSystemCode="0" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="041" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </dmRef> for a functional description of the frame system.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Wheel</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The wheel is the point of contact between the bicycle and the road for the bicycle to have movement. Refer to <dmRef>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA0" subSystemCode="0" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="041" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </dmRef> for a functional description of the wheel.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Spokes</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The spokes are thick wires with tension applied that connect the hub to the rim. You can adjust the tension with the nipple on the rim side.</para>
                        
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Hub</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The hub attaches to the center of the wheel where the axle and the bearings are.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Metal rim</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The metal rim is a metal ring that has a U-shaped cross section to hold the spokes on the inner side and the tire on the outer side.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Seat</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The seat, which is also known as the "saddle", is used as the support platform for the person to sit on the bicycle.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Seat post</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The seat post is used as a support post for the seat and to change the height of the seat for the rider.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Handle bar</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The handle bar is a horizontal bar with handles on each end. The handle bar is a steering mechanism that the rider uses to change the direction of the bicycle. The brake levers are also on the handle bar. Refer to <dmRef>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA2" subSystemCode="2" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="720" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </dmRef> for information on how to install the handle bar. Refer to <dmRef>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA2" subSystemCode="2" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="520" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </dmRef> for information on removing the handlebar.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Handle bar stem</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The handle bar stem (the stem) attaches the handle bar to the steering tube. Refer to <dmRef>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA2" subSystemCode="1" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="720" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </dmRef> for information on how to install a stem. Refer to <dmRef>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA2" subSystemCode="1" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="520" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </dmRef> for information on how to remove the stem.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Brake levers</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>When you operate the brake lever, the brake pads move against the wheel to decrease the speed. The brake lever on the left side operates the front brake. The brake lever on the right side operates the rear brake.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Brakes</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>When you operate the brakes, the brake pad moves against the wheel to decrease the speed of the bicycle. Refer to <dmRef>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA1" subSystemCode="0" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="041" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </dmRef> for a description of the braking system.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Shifters</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The shifters are the mechanisms that you use to change the gears on the bicycle. There are 7 different types of shifters that have been developed over the years, but they all have the same functionality. When you operate the shifters, they pull the control cable to move the derailleur towards a larger diameter chain ring. The shifters can also loosen the cable to let the derailleur move towards a smaller diameter chain ring. Refer to <dmRef>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA5" subSystemCode="3" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="041" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </dmRef> for a functional description of the shifters.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Crank</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The crank moves the power to the chain rings when the pedals operate.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Pedals</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The pedals move the force of movement from the feet to the cranks.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Chain</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The chain moves the power from the chain rings to the cogs on the freewheel. Refer to <dmRef>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA4" subSystemCode="1" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="251" infoCodeVariant="B" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </dmRef> for the procedure on how to clean the chain.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Gears</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The gears have different mechanisms that function together to change the speed of the bicycle. These mechanisms include: <randomList listItemPrefix="pf02">
                              <listItem>
                                 <para>the sprockets</para>
                              </listItem>
                              <listItem>
                                 <para>the chain</para>
                              </listItem>
                              <listItem>
                                 <para>the derailleur</para>
                              </listItem>
                           </randomList> Refer to <dmRef>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA5" subSystemCode="0" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="041" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </dmRef> for a functional description of the gear system.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Chain rings</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The chain rings (also known as the "chain wheel") pull on the chain when the cranks turn.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Derailleur</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>A derailleur moves the chain from one sprocket to another to change the gears. There are two different types of derailleur, the front and the rear. The highest ratio (highest gear) is when the chain is on the largest sprocket on the front and the smallest at the rear. To get the lowest gear, the smallest sprocket is at the front and the largest at the rear. Refer to <dmRef>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA5" subSystemCode="1" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="041" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </dmRef> for a functional description of the derailleur system.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
               </definitionList>
            </para>
         </levelledPara>
      </description>
   </content>
</dmodule>

      <description>
         <levelledPara>
            <title>Quick history of the bicycle</title>
            
            <para>Here are the most important steps in the invention of the bicycle:<sequentialList id="SPEC-0008">
                  <listItem>
                     <para>In 1817 a German professor, baron Karl von Drais, created the first two-wheeled bicycle. It had a handlebar, and looked like a bicycle of today, but it didn't have pedals, and it had a wooden body.</para>
                  </listItem>
                  <listItem>
                     <para>In the 1860s, French inventors added pedals to the front wheel. However, it took a lot of effort to turn the pedals. Later inventors made bikes out of metal only, and made the front wheel very big, giving higher speed. This design was called the penny-farthing bicycle. However, it was difficult to ride, since it could fall easily.</para>
                  </listItem>
                  <listItem>
                     <para>Several improvements were made in the 1880s and '90s. In 1885, the safety bicycle was invented. This had two wheels the same size so that the rider could sit at a lower height. It was called the safety bicycle because it was much easier to ride than the penny-farthing. Instead of pedaling and steering with the front wheel, the safety bicycle used steering with the front wheel while the pedals turned the back wheel using a chain. Brakes operated by hand levers on some bikes also increased safety.</para>
                  </listItem>
                  <listItem>
                     <para>In 1888, Scottish inventor John Boyd Dunlop re-invented a type of tire which was filled with air, and this made cycling far more comfortable.</para>
                  </listItem>
                  <listItem>
                     <para>Soon, the freewheel was invented. This was a device inside the hub of the back wheel that allowed the wheel to spin even if the rider wasn't pedalling. However, this meant the rider could no longer stop the bike by backpedalling. As a result, a different type of brake was invented which could stop the bike if the pedals were turned backwards. Later inventions included better brakes, and gears, which made cycling over hills much easier.</para>
                  </listItem>
                  <listItem>
                     <extra_id_45>
                        <extra_id_46>During this time the bicycle became very popular. Long-distance racing are quickly developing:<attentionSequentialList id="SPEC-0004">
                              <extra_id_47 id="SPEC-0005">
                                 <attentionListItemPara id="SPEC-0001">Paris-Rouen, as soon as 1869</attentionListItemPara>
                              </extra_id_47>
                              <extra_id_48>
                                 <extra_id_49>Bordeaux-Paris, in May 1891</extra_id_49>
                              </extra_id_48>
                              <attentionSequentialListItem>
                                 <attentionListItemPara>Paris-Brest-Paris, in September 1891</attentionListItemPara>
                              </attentionSequentialListItem>
                              <attentionSequentialListItem>
                                 <attentionListItemPara>Liège-Bastogne-Liège, in 1892</attentionListItemPara>
                              </attentionSequentialListItem>
                              <attentionSequentialListItem>
                                 <extra_id_50>Paris-Roubaix, in 1896</extra_id_50>
                              </attentionSequentialListItem>
                              <attentionSequentialListItem>
                                 <extra_id_51>Tour de France, in 1903</extra_id_51>
                              </attentionSequentialListItem>
                           </attentionSequentialList>
                        </extra_id_46>
                        
                     </extra_id_45>
                  </listItem>
               </sequentialList>
               <verbatimText id="SPEC-0009">Source: https://en.vikidia.org/w/index.php?title=Bicycle&oldid=97889</verbatimText>
            </para>
            
            <extra_id_52>
               <extra_id_53>Bicycles are nowadays one of the main means of transportation in many parts of the world. Its energy efficiency is particularly high. Its practice, cycling, is both<attentionRandomList>
                     <attentionRandomListItem id="SPEC-0003">
                        <attentionListItemPara id="SPEC-0002">a daily use of transport,</attentionListItemPara>
                     </attentionRandomListItem>
                     <attentionRandomListItem>
                        <attentionListItemPara>a popular hobby,</attentionListItemPara>
                     </attentionRandomListItem>
                     <attentionRandomListItem>
                        <attentionListItemPara>and a sport.</attentionListItemPara>
                     </attentionRandomListItem>
                  </attentionRandomList>
                  <extra_id_54 id="SPEC-0010">Source: https://fr.vikidia.org/w/index.php?title=V%C3%A9lo&oldid=1427276</extra_id_54>
               </extra_id_53>
               
            </extra_id_52>
         </levelledPara>
         <extra_id_55>
            <extra_id_56>Functional description of a bicycle</extra_id_56>
            <para>Below is a list of the different bicycle components and a functional description of them. <extra_id_57>
                  <definitionListHeader>
                     <extra_id_58>Component</extra_id_58>
                     <definitionTitle>Functional description</definitionTitle>
                  </definitionListHeader>
                  
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Frame</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The frame is the skeleton of the bicycle. Refer to <extra_id_59>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA3" subSystemCode="0" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="041" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </extra_id_59> for a functional description of the frame system.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Wheel</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The wheel is the point of contact between the bicycle and the road for the bicycle to have movement. Refer to <dmRef>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA0" subSystemCode="0" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="041" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </dmRef> for a functional description of the wheel.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Spokes</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The spokes are thick wires with tension applied that connect the hub to the rim. You can adjust the tension with the nipple on the rim side.</para>
                        
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <extra_id_60>
                     <listItemTerm>Hub</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The hub attaches to the center of the wheel where the axle and the bearings are.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </extra_id_60>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Metal rim</listItemTerm>
                     <extra_id_61>
                        <para>The metal rim is a metal ring that has a U-shaped cross section to hold the spokes on the inner side and the tire on the outer side.</para>
                     </extra_id_61>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <extra_id_62>
                     <extra_id_63>Seat</extra_id_63>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <extra_id_64>The seat, which is also known as the "saddle", is used as the support platform for the person to sit on the bicycle.</extra_id_64>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </extra_id_62>
                  <extra_id_65>
                     <listItemTerm>Seat post</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The seat post is used as a support post for the seat and to change the height of the seat for the rider.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </extra_id_65>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <extra_id_66>Handle bar</extra_id_66>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <extra_id_67>The handle bar is a horizontal bar with handles on each end. The handle bar is a steering mechanism that the rider uses to change the direction of the bicycle. The brake levers are also on the handle bar. Refer to <extra_id_68>
                              <extra_id_69>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA2" subSystemCode="2" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="720" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </extra_id_69>
                           </extra_id_68> for information on how to install the handle bar. Refer to <extra_id_70>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <extra_id_71 modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA2" subSystemCode="2" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="520" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </extra_id_70> for information on removing the handlebar.</extra_id_67>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <extra_id_72>Handle bar stem</extra_id_72>
                     <extra_id_73>
                        <extra_id_74>The handle bar stem (the stem) attaches the handle bar to the steering tube. Refer to <dmRef>
                              <extra_id_75>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA2" subSystemCode="1" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="720" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </extra_id_75>
                           </dmRef> for information on how to install a stem. Refer to <dmRef>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <extra_id_76 modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA2" subSystemCode="1" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="520" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </dmRef> for information on how to remove the stem.</extra_id_74>
                     </extra_id_73>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Brake levers</listItemTerm>
                     <extra_id_77>
                        <para>When you operate the brake lever, the brake pads move against the wheel to decrease the speed. The brake lever on the left side operates the front brake. The brake lever on the right side operates the rear brake.</para>
                     </extra_id_77>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <extra_id_78>Brakes</extra_id_78>
                     <extra_id_79>
                        <extra_id_80>When you operate the brakes, the brake pad moves against the wheel to decrease the speed of the bicycle. Refer to <dmRef>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA1" subSystemCode="0" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="041" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </dmRef> for a description of the braking system.</extra_id_80>
                     </extra_id_79>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <extra_id_81>Shifters</extra_id_81>
                     <extra_id_82>
                        <para>The shifters are the mechanisms that you use to change the gears on the bicycle. There are 7 different types of shifters that have been developed over the years, but they all have the same functionality. When you operate the shifters, they pull the control cable to move the derailleur towards a larger diameter chain ring. The shifters can also loosen the cable to let the derailleur move towards a smaller diameter chain ring. Refer to <dmRef>
                              <extra_id_83>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA5" subSystemCode="3" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="041" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </extra_id_83>
                           </dmRef> for a functional description of the shifters.</para>
                     </extra_id_82>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <extra_id_84>
                     <listItemTerm>Crank</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>The crank moves the power to the chain rings when the pedals operate.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </extra_id_84>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Pedals</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <extra_id_85>The pedals move the force of movement from the feet to the cranks.</extra_id_85>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <extra_id_86>Chain</extra_id_86>
                     <extra_id_87>
                        <extra_id_88>The chain moves the power from the chain rings to the cogs on the freewheel. Refer to <dmRef>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA4" subSystemCode="1" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="251" infoCodeVariant="B" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </dmRefIdent>
                           </dmRef> for the procedure on how to clean the chain.</extra_id_88>
                     </extra_id_87>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <extra_id_89>
                     <extra_id_90>Gears</extra_id_90>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <extra_id_91>The gears have different mechanisms that function together to change the speed of the bicycle. These mechanisms include: <randomList listItemPrefix="pf02">
                              <listItem>
                                 <extra_id_92>the sprockets</extra_id_92>
                              </listItem>
                              <listItem>
                                 <extra_id_93>the chain</extra_id_93>
                              </listItem>
                              <listItem>
                                 <para>the derailleur</para>
                              </listItem>
                           </randomList> Refer to <dmRef>
                              <extra_id_94>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA5" subSystemCode="0" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="041" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </extra_id_94>
                           </dmRef> for a functional description of the gear system.</extra_id_91>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </extra_id_89>
                  <definitionListItem>
                     <listItemTerm>Chain rings</listItemTerm>
                     <extra_id_95>
                        <para>The chain rings (also known as the "chain wheel") pull on the chain when the cranks turn.</para>
                     </extra_id_95>
                  </definitionListItem>
                  <extra_id_96>
                     <listItemTerm>Derailleur</listItemTerm>
                     <listItemDefinition>
                        <para>A derailleur moves the chain from one sprocket to another to change the gears. There are two different types of derailleur, the front and the rear. The highest ratio (highest gear) is when the chain is on the largest sprocket on the front and the smallest at the rear. To get the lowest gear, the smallest sprocket is at the front and the largest at the rear. Refer to <extra_id_97>
                              <extra_id_98>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="DA5" subSystemCode="1" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="041" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />
                              </extra_id_98>
                           </extra_id_97> for a functional description of the derailleur system.</para>
                     </listItemDefinition>
                  </extra_id_96>
               </extra_id_57>
            </para>
         </extra_id_55>
      </description>
   </content>
</dmodule>

If the chain is too dirty, clean it as specified in the clean chain task (refer to ). Visually examine the chain for links that are frozen or that do not move easily. Apply the necessary . Try to pull the chain away from the front of the chain ring. Make sure that the chain is not loose. Tighten the chain if, when you pull it away from the chain ring, you can see a full tooth. Tighten the chain with the Allen wrench from the .

                        </dmNode>
                        <dmNode>
                           <dmRef>
                              <dmRefIdent>
                                 <dmCode modelIdentCode="S1000DBIKE" systemDiffCode="AAA" systemCode="D00" subSystemCode="0" subSubSystemCode="0" assyCode="00" disassyCode="00" disassyCodeVariant="AA" infoCode="043" infoCodeVariant="A" itemLocationCode="A" />

                                       <variableRef variableName="tourCorrectAnswer" />

                  </proceduralStep>
